The `fortress-repo` skill (`compiler.md`, "The checker's time") gives the steps, their commands and what the rung reports.
62	- P-149 **An object that inherits an abstract functional method from one trait, and a body for it from a sibling trait, is refused unless it declares the method itself.** In `object O extends { A, B }`, where `A` declares `pick(self)` abstract and `B` gives `pick(self)` a body, `O` must declare its own `pick`. Scala's way, where the sibling trait's body implements the abstract method, is not taken. The compiled checker refuses such an object, as the specification's text and the type group's Welterweight calculus (`Papers/Welterweight/`) require. Walk already refuses it at load, by the Meet Rule for Functional Methods. A trait that declares one method both abstract and with a body, at the same parameter types, is refused too. Why: the revival honors the designers' intent. It changes Fortress's nature only to reconcile a conflict between the earlier and the later designers' choices, and then looks to other languages for how to do it. Here there is no such conflict, and Fortress is not bent to Scala's way for a hypothetical convenience.
63	- P-151 **Only the `where`-clause forms that the team wrote down are built: conditional extension, a function's or a method's condition, and `AnyList`'s `comprises` clause.** A `where` clause states conditions on static parameters, and may introduce static variables of its own, as `where [\E\]` does. A trait or object that extends a type under a `where` condition is that type only where the condition holds, and its members are checked with the condition holding (conditional extension). A `where` condition on a function's or a method's own static parameters bounds them. The team's commented-out clause `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]` becomes live, which clears the type error of `AnyList`'s join `||`; its other operations, `addLeft` and `addRight`, move into `List` (row 799). `SUM`'s fusion with `MAX` and `MIN`, the library's fast path for the maximum or the minimum of sums, stays. A method's `where` condition clears four of the fusion's six type errors; for the other two, the team's commented-out generic `distribute` is the fix measured (F-242 holds the measurement: as the team wrote it, it only moves them). Why: a feature with little support in the team's work bends the language beyond what the curator can review. He has such a feature built where the team left enough design intent for it, or where it is on the critical path to running fast compiled. Row 773: the members scoped to the condition, since a member checked under it stays callable where the condition fails. Row 774: walk's half of conditional extension. Row 701: the code generator's half.
64	- P-152 **Walk and the compiled checker read the exclusion of two generic declarations over their whole parameter types, by existential reduction.** With static parameters, the parameter types of two declarations can exclude each other as a whole, even where no single parameter excludes its counterpart. In `o[\T\](x: P[\T\], b: Box[\T\])` beside `o[\T\](x: Q[\T\], b: Box[\T\])`, where `P[\T\]` excludes `Q[\T\]` only at the same `T`, neither parameter excludes alone. But no value is a `Box` of two types, so `b` fixes the same `T` for both declarations, and no argument fits both. A generic trait in `Box`'s place fixes `T` in the same way. Both paths read such a pair as excluding, and judge it on that reading by the overloading rules (P-45: the 2011 paper's No Duplicates, Meet and Return Type rules). Why: the type group's 2011 paper decides exclusion between parameter types with static parameters by existential reduction (`Papers/Types/exc-reduction.tick`; P-26, the type group's later word outweighs the specification's early text), as the revised specification states (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`, "Declarations with Static Parameters"). Walk refuses such a pair at load where one declaration has a `where` clause, which the checker accepts (row 787); and walk reads an object type over a static parameter, such as `Box[\T\]`, as excluding a type that it equals at some instance, such as `Box[\ZZ32\]`, so that it loads a pair that the checker refuses (row 788).
65	- P-154 **A list is ordered only where its element type is totally ordered.** The library's `List` extends its lexicographic order only where its element type extends `StandardTotalOrder` (conditional extension, P-151). Floats and `QQ` are only partially ordered, since NaN, and `QQ`'s 0/0, compare with nothing. So on the compiled checker a list of floats or of `QQ` has no order: no `<`, `CMP` or the other comparisons, though its `=` stays. A pair of floats stays ordered: the curator accepted that mismatch as a cost of the list rule. The tuples' own rule is not decided here. No lexicographic trait over partially ordered elements is added now: the team never wrote one, and the case touches neither the distance to the switch-over nor microGPT. Why: the team's later code bounds the element of both of its lexicographic traits by a total order (`Library/incomplete/advanced/Fortress.PartialTotalOrders.fss:117-140`; P-26, the team's later word outweighs its early text), and conditional extension is a `where` form that the team wrote (P-151). Row 774: walk's half, since walk still gives every list an order.
66	- P-155 **The compiled checker checks the overloads of symbolic operators before the switch-over.** Today its overloading check reads an operator only if its name is a word of capitals, such as `MAX`, so `+`, `^`, `||`, the subscripts and the other symbolic operators pass unchecked. The check must read them by the rules that it applies to any function, so that the distance to the switch-over reaches zero with them checked. Why: the skip is a gap that the team knew, not a rule: the specification's appendix of proposed features calls the library's two subscript operators "not really a valid overloading" (`Specification/appendices/future.tex:186-207`, its item on array indexing). A zero with them unchecked would hide known errors. Each design that the check needs is brought to the curator before its rung, with the probe's measurement (`perf-probes/symbolic-operators-2/REPORT.md`); the two it found are decided: P-156, the subscripts' index bound, and P-157, vectors that are not additive groups. Row 584: the check and its rungs.
67	- P-156 **A collection's index type extends `Index`, a trait that the ranges exclude, and a tuple of indices is an `Index`.** Every index parameter of the library's generic indexed types is bounded `I extends Index`; `ZZ32` extends `Index`, and `Range` excludes it. So a subscript that takes one index and a subscript that takes a range never apply to the same value, and the pair is a valid overloading at every instance. A tuple type whose elements are all `Index` types is itself an `Index`, on both paths and in the specification: a typing rule that changes no value, so `m[i, j]` passes its tuple `(i, j)` as before. Why: it is the team's own fix for this pair (`Specification/appendices/future.tex:186-207`), its "magic" read as subtyping. A `where` constraint `I excludes Range[\I\]` was weighed and not taken: the team left such a constraint as an open question, and the code generator refuses a `where` clause in a declaration's header. Row 783: the subscript pair.
68	- P-157 **`Vector` and `Matrix` are not additive groups for now, so the arrays' scalar `+` and `-` stand beside the vectors' own.** They keep their own `+`, `-` and unary `-`, but no longer extend `AdditiveGroup`, and arrays exclude every additive group, as `Array3` already does. So generic code over `AdditiveGroup`, such as `SUM` over vectors or `zero`, no longer takes them. Why: the scalar block that microGPT uses (P-88) and the team's additive-group vectors cannot both pass the overload check while it reads a self-typed trait's `self` in a signature as the plain trait type (P-146); the library's consistency gives way, since it must not hold up microGPT. Vectors may become additive groups again once the checker reads `self` as the implementing type in the overload check.
69	
70	### Numbers
71	
72	- P-66 **The integer principle: Java's and the JVM's defaults stay where they make sense, and are corrected where they fail high performance or mathematical precision.** The team did so with rounding. A hardware behaviour that bytecode can express gets its own explicit spelling, as the specification's wrapping and saturating operators do. Where the JVM prevents a correct implementation, the project gives way for now. The peers to compare are Julia, X10, Swift and Rust.
73	- P-67 **`round` on an exact half goes to the even integer, on both paths.** Under walk and on the compiled path, `round(2.5)` gives 2: an `RR64` or `RR32` value rounds an exact half to the even integer, as a rational does. This is the specification's rule for rationals, the default rounding of IEEE 754, and the rule of the team's own `round` on rationals.
74	- P-68 **On the float types, `floor` and `ceiling` return the same float type, while the brackets ⌊x⌋ and ⌈x⌉, `round` and `truncate` return `ZZ`, the unbounded integer.** So `floor(2.5)` is the `RR64` value 2.0, and ⌊2.5⌋ is to be the `ZZ` value 2. Row 330: one library rung after the switch-over, which first counts the interpreter tests whose output changes, then makes the brackets, `round` and `truncate` return `ZZ` in each of the library's declarations of them; today the brackets are `ZZ64` under walk and `RR64` compiled, and `round` and `truncate` are `ZZ64`, `ZZ` or `RR64` by declaration.
75	- P-69 **`LSHIFT` and `RSHIFT` are bit operators on the fixed-width integer types, and `ZZ`'s `shift` is exact.** On `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32` and `NN64`, a shift loses the bits that it shifts out, silently, as in every peer language. A count at or beyond the width gives 0, or -1 for `RSHIFT` of a negative value, and a negative count shifts the other way, as Swift's and Julia's shifts do. The count may have any integer type, and the shift works at the width of the value shifted. On `ZZ`, the unbounded integers ℤ, `shift(x, k)` is ⌊x·2^k⌋ at any count; there the specification defines `x LSHIFT k` as `shift(x, k)` and `x RSHIFT k` as `shift(x, -k)`. On the compiled path, a shift of a fixed-width value works on the JVM's `int` or `long`, never through `ZZ`. Why: a shift through `ZZ` costs speed wherever the JVM cannot remove it. Row 442: the compiled `NN32` and `NN64` shifts, refused today. Row 383: `ZZ`'s `shift`, which the compiler's prelude does not declare. Row 381: a count of another integer type, where the compiled path refuses a `ZZ`, `NN32` or `NN64` count and computes a `ZZ64` count on a `ZZ32` at 64 bits.
76	- P-70 **`GCD` and `LCM` give nonnegative results, and `LCM` raises `IntegerOverflow` when the multiple does not fit its type.** So `0 GCD -4` is 4 and `1 LCM -5` is 5, and on `ZZ32`, `(2^31 - 1) LCM 2` raises. The rule applies on both paths. Why: the specification says that both results are nonnegative, and its general rule raises `IntegerOverflow` for an integer result that does not fit. The same general rule makes `GCD` raise it where the divisor does not fit, as in the specification's example `-2^31 GCD 0` on `ZZ32`. Row 442: `GCD` and `LCM` on the compiled path's `NN32` and `NN64`.
77	- P-71 **An overflow guard tests for the type's most negative value, not for `a = -a`, so `|0|`, `-0` and `0 DIV -1` do not overflow.** On a signed fixed-width type, only the most negative value overflows when it is negated, taken in absolute value or divided by -1. The test `a = -a` is true for that value, and also for 0. Walk already gave 0 in the three cases. On the compiled path, the natives of negation, absolute value and division on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64` test for the most negative value. The same faulty test sat in `ZZ64`'s multiplication, through which its `REM`, `MOD`, `GCD` and `LCM` compute, so `0 · 5`, `3 REM 5` and `12 GCD 18` raised; that multiplication now raises only when the exact product does not fit. Why: no reading of the specification makes the three cases overflow.
78	- P-72 **`narrow` keeps the low 32 bits of a value that the narrower type cannot hold, signed and unsigned, on both paths, and raises no `IntegerOverflow`.** The decision covers `narrow` from a `ZZ64` to a `ZZ32` and from an `NN64` to an `NN32`. A value that the narrower type holds is unchanged; any other becomes the value of the narrower type with the same low 32 bits. Why: the team's specification said nothing on `narrow`, and the team's boundary test `ProjectFortress/tests/UnsignedTest.fss` asserts the low 32 bits for `NN64` values. On the unsigned types, keeping the low bits is a bit operation, like a shift, and the signed `narrow` gets the same answer.
79	- P-73 **Under walk, fixed-width integer arithmetic raises `IntegerOverflow` when its result does not fit, on the unsigned `NN32` and `NN64` too.** The rule covers every operation whose result can leave its type, `^`, `CHOOSE` and `LCM` included (F-132 holds what is built and its tests). So a subtraction below 0 on `NN32` raises. Code that means to wrap uses the specification's wrapping operators ∔ (`DOTPLUS`), ∸ (`DOTMINUS`) and ⨰ (`DOTTIMES`), fully parenthesised, since the specification states their precedence only among the three. The specification's saturating operators, such as ⊞ (`BOXPLUS`), are not in the interpreter's library; they come in a later step of their own (row 797). Why: this is the specification's rule, and the compiled path already raised the error for addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, negation and absolute value on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64`. The decision is walk's. On the compiled path the rule holds as the specification's (P-25, the standard), and the compiled path departs from it at `^` (rows 523 to 525) and at `CHOOSE` (row 521).
80	- P-74 **Mixed integer widths convert by declared coercions: each wider integer type declares a `coerce` from each narrower integer type, as the compiler prelude does.** A conversion that is exact is implicit, and a conversion that can lose precision is written out. So `ZZ32` values and integer numerals coerce into `RR64` implicitly, and a `ZZ64` value into `RR64` is written out (P-66, Java's defaults corrected where they lose precision). A call of a generic function with arguments of mixed widths infers, on both paths, the narrowest type into which its arguments coerce. A range is over `ZZ32` only (P-77, the rule on ranges). The specification's `widens` declaration, which would make a narrow computation stored into a wide variable run wide, is deferred. The implicit coercion of `NN32` into `RR64`: P-75 holds it, with its conflict with the overloads of `RR64` and `ZZ64`.
81	- P-75 **`NN32` coerces into `RR64` implicitly, since every `NN32` value converts to `RR64` exactly.** Why: a conversion that fits is implicit, the rule of P-74 on mixed widths. With the coercion, an operator that both `RR64` and `ZZ64` declare is ambiguous on both paths for a `ZZ32` with an `NN32`, since neither `ZZ64` nor `RR64` coerces into the other. Without it, P-74's rule, the narrowest type into which both arguments coerce, gives `ZZ64`. Row 575: the coercion, which the tree lacks, with this conflict and its measurement. Each way to build it changes a decided behaviour, so the choice of a way is not a worker's (`fortress-repo`'s exploring part).
82	- P-76 **An integer numeral has a type of its own, `IntLiteral`, which each number type converts from: in the interpreter's library now, and under walk once walk has the checker's static types.** The design is the compiler's prelude's working one, taken in place of the specification's numeral types, which the team left unfinished. Why the split: walk has no static types, so it would give a list of numerals the element type `IntLiteral`, with no declared type to go by. The interpreter's library declares `IntLiteral`, the conversions from it into the five integer types, `QQ` and `RR64`, and `IntLiteral`'s own arithmetic, which the team had left commented out until coercion existed. Walk still gives an integer numeral the type `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit, so no numeral reaches `IntLiteral`'s declarations under walk. Walk gaps: a numeral that walk matches as a `ZZ32` in a `typecase` or an overload (row 79), a numeral at an `NN32` or `NN64` binding (row 454), an integer numeral beyond `ZZ32`'s range at an `RR64` binding (row 443), a `nat` parameter used as a value (row 486), and coercion through tuple and varargs parameters (rows 395 and 511).
83	- P-77 **Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only, as the compiler's prelude declares them (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`).** Why: a JVM array has at most as many elements as the largest `ZZ32`. A range over another integer type is a static error. A loop whose counter needs a wider type runs over a `ZZ32` range and widens each element, as in `j: ZZ64 = i`. A range of rank 2 or 3 is a tuple of `ZZ32` scalar ranges. The public range traits, such as `Range[\I\]`, stay generic in their index type: the ranges of rank 2 and 3 extend them at pairs and triples of `ZZ32`.
84	- P-78 **`SUM` and `PROD` are one generic reduction each over the library's algebra, in place of the team's catch-all over `Number`, and take their identity from the static argument.** `SUM` is generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `PROD` over `MultiplicativeRing`. A reduction written with generators writes its static argument where nothing at the call fixes the element type. The compiled checker fixes it from neither the generators, the body nor a declared type that receives the value, and refuses every such `SUM` or `PROD` that leaves it out (row 731, a gap of the checker). Row 731's workaround is to write it in every clause form of `SUM` and `PROD`, as in `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. A sum without generators is written as before, with no static argument: `SUM e` over a collection `e`, and the dot product `x DOT y`. `BIG MAXN`, `BIG MINN` and `BIG MINMAXN`, the team's `Number`-typed big operators for the maximum, the minimum and both, each with an identity, are gone; no program called them. `MAX` and `MIN` get no identity on the integers or the floats, so an empty `BIG MAX` or `BIG MIN` raises `EmptyReduction` (F-60: a maximum's identity is its type's least value, which a coercion into a wider type does not carry). Under walk, an empty `SUM` or `PROD` over another algebra, such as a user `AdditiveGroup`, still fails (row 436) until the specification's `HasIdentity` is built.
85	- P-79 **Every team demo is kept running as the tree changes.** The team demos are the programs in `ProjectFortress/demos/`; no suite or step of the gate runs them. If a change breaks a demo and the way to repair the demo is known, the batch that makes the change also rewrites the demo. A batch is a set of tasks, each called a rung, that agents build at once and land together. For example, the change that made `10^(-4)` an error (P-153, the integer power) also wrote `10.0^(-4)` in `BiCGSTAB.fss` and `BiCGSTAB2.fss`, and `10.0^(-6)` for `10^(-6)` in `npbft.fss`. A demo that fails for want of a feature is made to run again once the feature is built. So the demos known to fail today are to be respelled where the way is known: the five demos that walk refuses at load, since they leave an inherited abstract method without a body (row 670, which names them); `trips.fss`, which walk runs but the compiled checker refuses, since its `generator` object extends `StandardTotalOrder[\trip\]` without being a `trip` (row 710); the timing line of `BiCGSTAB.fss` and `BiCGSTAB2.fss`, which divides a `ZZ64` by a float and so stops walk (row 791); and the reductions that the compiled checker refuses because they leave out the static argument of a big operator whose bound names its own static parameter, such as `SUM`; their repair writes the argument (row 731).
86	- P-80 **The specification's sign-refined number types are a superseded design: a program tests such a subset of a type at run time.** These types are the specification's subtypes by sign, such as positive ℚ, non-negative ℚ and non-zero ℚ, and the same refinements of the integers. The machine types `NN32` and `NN64` are separate types, not among them. The specification's number chapters now test a value's sign by comparison, and a float with two getters of `RR64`: `check` returns `Just(x)` for a finite `x`, `check_star` returns `Just(x)` for an `x` that is not a NaN, and each returns `Nothing` otherwise. The chapter that held the design, `Specification/advanced-lib/numbers-advanced.tex`, stays word for word, marked superseded by a callout in the form of every specification change (P-96), so that the original design stays on record. Their possible return belongs to P-62: once the `covariant` keyword is built, a worker tries to bring them back as covariant static parameters.
87	- P-153 **The integer power splits on the base: an integer base gives an integer or raises an error, and a float or rational base gives the fraction.** Each integer type's `^` returns its own type at every exponent. At a negative exponent, the bases 1 and -1 give their exact power, a base of 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and any other base raises `IntegerOverflow`. A program that wants a fraction writes a float or rational base, as in `2.0^(-1)`. Why: the team's later code gives an integer power the type of its integer base at a signed exponent (P-26, the team's later work outweighs the specification's early text). Overloads choose by type, and no type tells a negative exponent from a non-negative one, since a signed integer or a numeral can be either. So the split is on the base, and the sign of the exponent is tested at run time, as the library tests a value's sign everywhere (P-80, run-time sign tests in place of sign-refined types). Row 441: the same rule on the compiled path, whose own powers give 0 at a negative exponent and a raw Java exception at a base of 0, and overflow silently or with a raw Java exception (row 523).
88	
89	### Arrays and the model program
90	
91	- P-84 **An `RR64` array is stored as a Java `double[]`, unboxed, and arrays keep the team's `nat` sizes in their types.** Why: a high-performance language cannot box its array elements, and the sizes are central to the team's design. So the storage and the sizes are one design: the sizes stay in the array types as `nat` static parameters, as the library's `Vector` and `Matrix` declare them, and the compiled checker checks them. The sizes do not wait while a first version of the store carries them only as run-time fields; that layered plan was rejected. Both halves follow the library's own patterns (P-27, the library's own practice is the standard). The compiled checker checks `nat` static parameters (F-67). The compiled path's `double[]` store waits with the other array decisions until after the switch-over; among them is decision A, how an `RR64` array made through the library's generic array traits gets that store (P-85).

1	# Extract: Park, Hong, Steele & Ryu, "Polymorphic Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with Variance" (POPL 2019)
2	
3	Working notes on Gyunghee Park (KAIST and Oracle Labs), Jaemin Hong (KAIST),
4	Guy L. Steele Jr. (Oracle Labs) and Sukyoung Ryu (KAIST), *Polymorphic
5	Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with Variance*, Proc. ACM Program. Lang. 3, POPL,
6	Article 11, January 2019, 28 pages, doi:10.1145/3290324. These notes are our
7	own summary and commentary with brief attributed quotations, not a
8	reproduction of the paper.
9	
10	- **Source.** https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3290324. The PDF,
11	  https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/3290324?download=true, was downloaded by
12	  Pavol on 2026-09-29. It is 28 pages, SHA-256
13	  `791f978e529b17d533e3342763ed6c54a2f1027eeee5aac9869956b5cdd2b954`.
14	- **Copies in the repository.** The PDF is `research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019.pdf`
15	  (the same SHA-256) and its full text (`pdftotext -layout`) is
16	  `research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019.txt`, beside these notes, so that the paper's
17	  figures and rules are read at the source.
18	- **The copy the record read on 2026-09-23** (`explorations/reviews/mie-probes/literature.md`):
19	  http://web.archive.org/web/20240415191855/https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/3290324.
20	- **License**, as printed on the first page: "This work is licensed under a
21	  Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International License. ©
22	  2019 Copyright held by the owner/author(s)." That license permits
23	  copying and redistribution for non-commercial purposes with attribution.
24	  On that license and because the work needs the paper's figures at the
25	  source, the curator made it the exception to the rule that keeps copyrighted
26	  PDFs out of the repository (`explorations/protocol.md`, the hard rules).
27	
28	Page numbers are the printed article pages (11:N). The full proofs are in a
29	companion report, "Polymorphic Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with Variance
30	(Extended Report)", 2018, which the paper cites without a URL; the paper
31	itself gives proof sketches. Cross-references to this repository are marked
32	**[repo]**.
33	
34	## 1. What the paper is
35	
36	The abstract claims "the first formal specification of a strongly typed
37	object-oriented language with symmetric multiple dispatch, multiple
38	inheritance, and parametric polymorphism with variance", with a static and a
39	dynamic semantics and a type soundness proof "demonstrating that our novel
40	dynamic dispatch algorithm is consistent with the static semantics"
41	(p. 11:1). The calculus is **FGFV**, "Featherweight Generic Fortress with
42	Variance" (p. 11:3). It formalises the overloading rules of the 2011 OOPSLA
43	paper (Allen et al., in the tree as `Papers/Types/`), which were stated
44	informally and without a language semantics. It adds declaration-site
45	variance and a dispatch algorithm, and proves that the static rules and the
46	run-time choice agree (§6, p. 11:25).
47	
48	The language (Fig. 2, p. 11:8; §3.2, pp. 11:8-9):
49	- **Traits and objects.** Traits are "like Java interfaces that do not have
50	  any fields", and objects are "like Java final classes that cannot be
51	  extended".
52	- **Type parameters.** Trait type parameters carry a variance mark (`+`, `-`,
53	  `=`) and upper bounds. Object type parameters are always invariant. Method
54	  type parameters have lower and upper bounds, and the defaults are `Any` and
55	  `Bottom`.
56	- **Expressions.** Variables, first-class functions, object creation with
57	  written type arguments, and method calls `e.m(e)` with no written type
58	  arguments.
59	- **Types.** `Bottom` "is intentionally not expressible in the surface
60	  syntax" (p. 11:9). Union and intersection types exist only as internal
61	  types (p. 11:9). Tuples are not values.
62	- **What is left out.** "FGFV omits functional methods … and declarations
63	  of closed types …, but these could be added back to FGFV in an obvious
64	  way" (p. 11:3). Related work adds "modularity, nominal exclusion, and
65	  closed types" to that list (p. 11:25). There are no top-level functions:
66	  what is overloaded is methods.
67	
68	## 2. The rule excluding multiple instantiations
69	
70	- **The rule.** Every pair of a class's proper ancestors must satisfy
71	  [Anc-Diff-Trait] (instances of two different traits: no condition) or
72	  [Anc-Same-Trait] (Fig. 4, p. 11:11). [D-Trait] and [D-Object] both check it
73	  (Fig. 3, p. 11:10). [Anc-Same-Trait] requires that "if a class C extends two
74	  instances of a trait T, T⟦α⟧ and T⟦ρ⟧, then C also extends some T⟦γ⟧
75	  (which may be T⟦α⟧, T⟦ρ⟧, or a third instance) that extends both"
76	  (p. 11:11).
77	- **Per variance (our derivation from the rule's two subtype premises).** An
78	  invariant parameter forces γ = α = ρ, so two different instances cannot
79	  both be ancestors: that is the blanket rule. A covariant parameter needs an
80	  ancestor instance whose argument is below both arguments, and a
81	  contravariant one needs one whose argument is above both.
82	- **Why.** "Because the rules guarantee that there always exists a single
83	  minimal ancestor when a class extends multiple instances of a trait, no
84	  ambiguous method calls are possible due to multiple instances of a trait"
85	  (p. 11:11).
86	- **Credited.** The discussion calls it "the 'Ancestor Meet Rule' …
87	  introduced into Fortress in 2012 by Guy Steele and David Chase … to design
88	  an expressive type system with union and intersection types". It gives the
89	  laws T⟦α ⊓ α′⟧ ≡ T⟦α⟧ ⊓ T⟦α′⟧ for a covariant T and T⟦α ⊔ α′⟧ ≡ T⟦α⟧ ⊓
90	  T⟦α′⟧ for a contravariant one, and not "the 'obvious other two cases'"
91	  (p. 11:24). The citation is "Personal communication".
92	- **Used by the overloading check.** To close part of the gap between
93	  subtyping of domains and inclusion of applicable sets, the checker reduces
94	  an existential domain by collecting the constraints that keep it from being
95	  `Bottom` (*existential reduction*, pp. 11:13-14). The worked case uses
96	  invariance: with `ArrayList` extending `List` and both invariant, subtypes
97	  of `ArrayList⟦P⟧` and `List⟦Q⟧` "are exclusive unless they are both
98	  ArrayList⟦S⟧ for some type S" (pp. 11:13-14). So the rule is what lets
99	  two generic declarations be proved disjoint or nested.
100	- **Not argued.** The paper argues that the rule is sufficient, not that it
101	  is necessary.
102	
103	## 3. Variance
104	
105	- **Subtyping.** Declaration-site variance on trait type parameters, as in
106	  the example "T⟦U2, U1, U1⟧ <: T⟦U1, U2, U1⟧" for `trait T⟦+P, -Q, =S⟧` with
107	  U2 <: U1 (p. 11:9).
108	- **Positions.** [D-Method] checks that covariant and contravariant class
109	  type parameters appear only in positions of their own variance. A *type
110	  context* gives each position a variance: arrow domains and contravariant
111	  arguments flip it, and "type parameters of objects and invariant type
112	  parameters of traits are invariant" (pp. 11:11-12).
113	- **The overloading rules do not change.** "The overloading rules for FGF
114	  remain the same because covariant or contravariant types affect only the
115	  well-formedness of method declarations rather than the validity of
116	  overloading" (p. 11:12).
117	- **Run time is where variance costs something.** "Supporting variance in a
118	  type-sound manner requires keeping track of the static types of method
119	  invocations at run time" (p. 11:7).
120	  - The example: `sort(x: ListC⟦A⟧)`, `sort(x: ListC⟦B⟧)` and
121	    `sort⟦P⟧(x: ListC⟦C⟧): SortedListI⟦P⟧`, with `ListC` covariant and
122	    `SortedListI` invariant, beside a generic
123	    `merge⟦P⟧(SortedListI⟦P⟧, SortedListI⟦P⟧)`.
124	  - Two calls statically typed `SortedListI⟦A⟧` feed a merge. If run time
125	    instantiates the third `sort`'s `P` as anything but `A`, "the merge call
126	    would fail, despite the fact that the program successfully passed static
127	    type checking" (p. 11:7).
128	- **The 2012 alternatives.** The team considered dropping contravariance,
129	  treating arrow domains as invariant and compensating "by introducing rules
130	  of coercion". They also considered dropping union types, and perhaps
131	  intersections, for pseudo-joins and pseudo-meets. The paper instead
132	  accepts "the potential for exponential blowup" at run time (p. 11:24).
133	
134	## 4. How dispatch picks among overloads
135	
136	### 4.1 The static rules (§4, pp. 11:12-15)
137	
138	- **The reading of a generic declaration.** Following Allen et al. 2011, a
139	  generic declaration is "a single declaration whose domain type is
140	  existentially quantified over its type parameters", not "a set of
141	  infinitely many monomorphic declarations" (p. 11:3). "A monomorphic method
142	  declaration is a generic method declaration without any type parameter"
143	  (p. 11:5).
144	- **Specificity.** The informal rules compare applicable sets, "which is not
145	  practically checkable", so the formal ones compare domain types by
146	  subtyping (p. 11:12). This is sound but "not complete" (p. 11:13), and
147	  existential reduction narrows the gap (§2 above).
148	- **Three rules for every pair of same-named declarations** (Fig. 5,
149	  p. 11:13):
150	  - No Duplicates: the two domains are not each below the other; either
151	    [No-Dup-Not-Less] or [No-Dup-Not-Gtr] suffices, so the rule refuses
152	    exactly a pair whose domains are mutual subtypes (p. 11:12).
153	  - Meet: the domains exclude ([Meet-Excl], their intersection reduces to
154	    `Bottom`), or one is below the other, or a third declaration's domain is
155	    equivalent to their intersection ([Meet-Third]).
156	  - Return Type ([Return-Test]): when d1 is more specific than d2,
157	    `arrow(d1)` must be a subtype of `∀⟦κ, κ′⟧((α ⊓ α′) → ρ′)`, where the
158	    κ are both declarations' type parameters, α and α′ their domains and ρ′
159	    the less specific return type.
160	- **What [Return-Test] guarantees.** It checks the informal rule "for any
161	  instance of d2 instantiated with σ2 that is applicable to γ, there exists
162	  an instance of d1 … that is applicable to γ and has a return type that is
163	  a subtype of the return type of the instance of d2" (p. 11:15). That is,
164	  it quantifies over every instance of the less specific declaration.
165	- **Theorem 4.1** (p. 11:15). "For any method invocation, there always
166	  exists a unique most specific method declaration in its set of applicable
167	  method declarations." No Duplicates makes specificity antisymmetric, and
168	  the Meet Rule gives "a meet for every nonempty subset".
169	- **Static resolution** ([T-Method], [MSAV], Fig. 7, p. 11:16). The checker
170	  picks an instance of the most specific declaration applicable to the static
171	  argument types, and annotates the call with that instance's return type.
172	  The type-annotated expression `ϵ.m(ϵ): α` is what runs.
173	
174	### 4.2 The dynamic choice (§5.2, pp. 11:16-21)
175	
176	- **The contract.** "dynamic overloading resolution then must select an
177	  instance of the most specific method declaration that is applicable to the
178	  dynamic types of the arguments and whose return type is a subtype of the
179	  static type of the expression" (p. 11:15).
180	- **Types at run time.** Types are reified: "all the type parameters are
181	  instantiated with ground types at run time", and a value's run-time type is
182	  its *ilk* (p. 11:17). Ground types include unions and intersections
183	  (Fig. 8, p. 11:17).
184	- **[R-Method]** (p. 11:17). It sorts the visible declarations most-to-least
185	  specific ("This order is statically determinable, so the sorting can be
186	  done at compile time"). It then runs the *dispatch semipredicate* on each
187	  declaration in turn and takes the first that succeeds. The receiver's ilk is
188	  matched together with the arguments' ilks, which is what makes the dispatch
189	  symmetric.
190	- **The semipredicate** ([Dispatch], pp. 11:17-18) has three steps:
191	  1. match the argument ilks against the domain to get lower and upper bounds
192	     for the method type parameters;
193	  2. match the call's static return type against the declared return type to
194	     get bounds "to make sure that the dynamic dispatch preserves type";
195	  3. solve the bounds.
196	
197	  "If any of these steps fails, the semipredicate is false: the declaration
198	  is not applicable" (p. 11:18). Matching a union can yield several candidate
199	  bound lists, combined as a Cartesian product (pp. 11:18-19).
200	- **Solving** (Fig. 10, p. 11:19). The rule works from the rightmost type
201	  parameter to the left and "computes a substitution … by taking the
202	  intersection of the upper bounds", declared and computed. It then
203	  propagates the choice into the declared lower bounds of the parameters to
204	  its left. It "never instantiates method type parameters with Bottom". The
205	  right-to-left pass works because of the binding restrictions (p. 11:11):
206	  - a method type parameter's scope "extends to the right of its
207	    declaration";
208	  - "no reference to a method type parameter appears in any of the upper
209	    bounds";
210	  - the union of the lower bounds must be below the intersection of the upper
211	    bounds.
212	- **The worked example** (§5.2.4, pp. 11:20-21).
213	  - Two covariant `append` declarations, over `SortedList` and over `List`.
214	  - The call has static type `List⟦C3⟧` and argument ilks `SortedCons⟦C1⟧`
215	    and `Cons⟦C2⟧`, with C1, C2 <: C3.
216	  - The `SortedList` declaration fails on the second argument, so the `List`
217	    one runs, instantiated at `[C3/P, C3/Q]`.
218	  - So the instance comes from the static return type's upper bound, not from
219	    the ilks' C1 and C2.
220	- **Why intersection of upper bounds.** The Fortress team "had assumed …
221	  that once the tightest possible upper and lower bounds for a method type
222	  parameter have been found, then the union (or pseudo-union) of the lower
223	  bounds should be chosen". For that and for a hybrid "we were unable to
224	  complete the proofs of correctness", so the algorithm "always chooses the
225	  intersection of the upper bounds" (p. 11:25).
226	- **Union instances.** A type parameter can be instantiated at a union at
227	  run time. In the paper's example `O.m(3, true): (Int ⊔ Boolean)`, "P of m
228	  is inferred as (Int ⊔ Boolean) by the dispatch semipredicate at run time"
229	  (p. 11:21).
230	
231	## 5. The run-time check on the return type
232	
233	- **What it is.** Every call carries its static return type into run time
234	  (§5.1, p. 11:16). Dispatch uses it as an upper bound when it instantiates
235	  the chosen declaration (p. 11:18).
236	- **It never moves a call to another declaration.**
237	  - Lemma 5.8: whatever instance the checker chose, "there exists a
238	    type-safe most specific method instance at run time" (p. 11:22). Its proof
239	    is where [Return-Test] is used (pp. 11:22-23).
240	  - Lemma 5.9: the first-dispatchable scan then yields an instance of the
241	    most specific declaration applicable to the ilks, with a return type below
242	    the static one (p. 11:23).
243	  - In a well-formed program the return-type bounds therefore never rule out
244	    that declaration. They only choose its instance.
245	- **What it costs.**
246	  - "In simple invariant cases, we expect the run-time cost to be relatively
247	    low but nonzero", since matching `List⟦String⟧` against `List⟦T⟧` only
248	    binds T (pp. 11:24-25).
249	  - For the covariant and contravariant cases, "caching or dynamic
250	    recompilation … may help" (p. 11:25).
251	  - The discussion calls left-to-right scoping "a relatively small sacrifice
252	    of expressivity for a large gain in dynamic efficiency" (p. 11:24).
253	
254	## 6. What it proves and what it leaves open
255	
256	**Proved (sketched here, full proofs in the companion report):**
257	- Theorem 4.1: a unique most specific declaration exists (p. 11:15).
258	- Soundness and completeness of type matching and of solving (Lemmas 5.1 to
259	  5.4), and so of the dispatch semipredicate (Theorems 5.5, 5.6;
260	  pp. 11:21-22). Completeness of matching assumes that a matched type holds
261	  no `Bottom` and no type parameter inside a union or intersection. The
262	  paper shows that every use meets this: declared types have neither, and
263	  unions reach a declaration only through already-ground instances
264	  (pp. 11:21-22).
265	- Lemmas 5.7 to 5.9 (pp. 11:22-23).
266	- Theorem 5.10, soundness of a method call: a well-typed call is reduced by
267	  [R-Method] and its body's type is below the call's static type (p. 11:23).
268	- Theorem 5.11, type soundness: if `e` types to `(ϵ, д)` and `ϵ` evaluates to
269	  a value, the value's type is below `д` (p. 11:24).
270	- Only the method-invocation case is proved, "the other cases are
271	  conventional" (p. 11:23). The proofs are not mechanised; the Coq model in
272	  the lineage is Kim and Ryu 2011, without generics (p. 11:4).
273	
274	**Left open or left out:**
275	- No static inference algorithm: "we do not present a specific static type
276	  inference algorithm that finds the substitution σ in rule [E-Sub]". The
277	  paper conjectures that its match rule could serve (p. 11:25).
278	- Domain subtyping is incomplete against applicable sets (p. 11:13).
279	- Exponential blowup is possible at run time (p. 11:24).
280	- The union-of-lower-bounds instance is unproved (p. 11:25).
281	- Functional methods and top-level functions, closed types (`comprises`),
282	  nominal exclusion (`excludes`) and modularity are out; the paper says they
283	  "could be added back … in an obvious way" but shows nothing (pp. 11:3,
284	  11:25). Self types and a numeric tower are absent: neither is mentioned,
285	  and `Integer` appears only in a `List⟦Integer⟧` example (p. 11:2).
286	- Method type parameters may not appear in upper bounds, so F-bounded method
287	  parameters are outside the calculus (p. 11:11). Trait parameters' bounds are
288	  checked in an environment that binds the parameters themselves ([D-Trait],
289	  p. 11:10), so by the rule's form F-bounded trait parameters are admitted.
290	- Whether the ancestor rule is necessary is not argued.
291	
292	## 7. How it differs from the 2012 Welterweight draft and Naden's write-ups
293	
294	The paper cites neither text; its only 2012 source is "Steele and Chase 2012.
295	Personal communication" (p. 11:28). The lineage is by content.
296	
297	**Welterweight** (`Papers/Welterweight/`: "Dynamic Dispatch and Type Inference
298	Semipredicates", Chase, Hilburn, Luchangco, Naden, Ryu, Steele, Tristan,
299	"PAPER SUBMITTED TO 2012 ACM SPLASH---OOPSLA", `paper.tick:499-509`; Naden
300	calls it "the failed OOPSLA 2012 submission",
301	`Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex:538`).
302	
303	- *The same:*
304	  - the Ancestors Meet Rule and its reason, a "unique minimal instance" for
305	    efficient dispatch (`static.tick:83-89`);
306	  - ilks;
307	  - the most-to-least-specific order with a first-success scan of dispatch
308	    semipredicates (`dispatch.tick:5-20`);
309	  - right-to-left processing of type parameters under left-to-right scoping
310	    (`dispatch.tick:67`).
311	- *The differences:*
312	  - **Inputs to dispatch.** Welterweight dispatches on the ilks alone: it is
313	    "possible to select the dynamically most specific applicable function or
314	    method from an overload set using only the ilks of the argument values; no
315	    other information about the arguments is needed" (`evaluation.tick:30-33`).
316	    POPL adds the call's static return type.
317	  - **The instance.** Welterweight aims at "the most specific instantiation"
318	    by propagating lower limits (`dispatch.tick:67`). It leaves the Return
319	    Type Rule to "one final adjustment step … after the entrypoint [has] been
320	    chosen", with no static type to adjust to (`dispatch.tick:212`). POPL
321	    takes the intersection of the upper bounds, the static return type among
322	    them.
323	  - **Proof.** Welterweight states soundness as propositions that "should
324	    also hold" if "our type system is sound" (`evaluation.tick:71-99`). POPL
325	    proves them.
326	  - **Language.** Welterweight's is larger: top-level functions, a typecase
327	    (`R-Match-Succeeds`), `comprises` and `excludes` clauses, and coverage of
328	    abstract declarations. POPL drops all of these. POPL does handle
329	    contravariance and intersections in matching, where Welterweight's main
330	    algorithm is "Simplified version: no contravariance or ∩", with
331	    contravariance a variation (`dispatch.tick:62`, `:365`).
332	  - **Self types.** Welterweight's self-typed-generics dispatch step is
333	    commented out (`dispatch.tick:195-210`); POPL has no self types at all.
334	
335	**Naden, "The Return Type Rule and Generics"** (2012-08-31,
336	`Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex`).
337	- *Rejected:* letting the static context limit which definitions are
338	  applicable, so that overloads failing the Return Type Rule could pass.
339	  "By adding contextual information to the concept of the overload set, we
340	  muddy its semantics" (`:241-305`, quoted at `:289-290`).
341	- *Kept:* the Return Type Rule, plus multiple instantiation exclusion: "any
342	  type which is a subtype of two distinct instantiations of a single generic
343	  type is equivalent to Bottom" (`:342-347`), with a proof (`:433`).
344	- *Why:* a canonical instance for run-time choice (`headOrID`, "Context
345	  does not give us any clue", `:480-495`). So "Fortress implements blanket
346	  multiple instantiation exclusion" (`:496`).
347	- *For covariant parameters:* a minimal instance suffices, "the ancestor
348	  meet rule that appears in the failed OOPSLA 2012 submission" (`:512-538`).
349	  He adds a second, cross-instantiation restriction between a covariant
350	  subtrait and its supertrait (`:540-566`). He finds that the numeric tower's
351	  self-type idiom breaks it, and that "more work needs to be done"
352	  (`:568-633`). His suggested rewrite puts the self type in a bound,
353	  `add⟦X <: Ring⟦X⟧⟧(X, X): X` (`:620-624`).
354	
355	**Naden, "Enforcing Fortress' Return Type Rule at Runtime"** (2012-08-31,
356	`Papers/RuntimeInstantiation/RTRinstantionTheory.tex`, with the notes of
357	May to July 2012 beside it).
358	- *Proposed:* adding bounds from the call's static return type to run-time
359	  instantiation "without changing which function definition will be chosen"
360	  (`:73-80`).
361	- *Proved:* a theorem that under the Return Type Rule the return-type bounds
362	  are satisfiable exactly when applicability is, so they can join the
363	  single pass (`:279-298`).
364	- *Not done:* the bound-generation algorithm and the open coding (`:84-89`).
365	
366	**POPL 2019 against these.**
367	- It carries out the second write-up in a full calculus, with proofs: the
368	  return-type bounds in the semipredicate, and Lemmas 5.8 and 5.9.
369	- It stays within the first write-up's position: overload sets are validated

373	- It does not do what that write-up rejected: the static type chooses the

=== justificationOfRTR.tex 480-640 ===
On the other hand, when we consider the runtime system, we realize that there is a strong
benefit to multiple instantiation exclusion.  It guarantees that for any type that extends a generic
trait, there exists a canonical instantiation of that trait for that object.  This is important for
overloads such as\\

$\begin{array}{l}
{\it headOrID}({\tt Object}) : {\tt Object}~(*){\it def1}\\
{\it headOrID}\ob{X}({\tt List}\ob{X}) : X~(*){\it def2}\\
\end{array}$\\

If {\it def1} is all that is known at compile time, but at runtime the object is a 
{\tt ConfusedList}, which instantiation of {\it def2} is used, {\tt Bit} or {\tt String}?
Context does not give us any clue because we only need an {\tt Object}.  Thus,
we need to choose an instantiation without any means to do so.  Outlawing this
type of overload is a slippery slope into special cases.

Ultimately, Fortress implements blanket multiple instantiation exclusion for the semantic
benefits and the simplicity of the restriction.

\section{Variant Generics}

In the above sections, we assumed that generics were {\it invariant} in the sense that $T\ob{X} <: T\ob{Y}$ if and only if $X = Y$.  However,
many abstractions can support more permissive subtyping between generic instantiations.   Fortress
supports variant generic types, including

\begin{enumerate}
\item {\bf Covariance}: $T\ob{X} <: T\ob{Y}$ if and only if $X <: Y$
\item {\bf Contravariance}: $T\ob{X} <: T\ob{Y}$ if and only if $Y <: X$
\end{enumerate}

We deal explicitly with covariance only as for our purposes, contravariance is the same with the subtyping relationship switched.

\subsection{Covariant multiple instantiation exclusion}

We need to update the definition of multiple instantiation exclusion to include covariant generic types.
We could leave the restriction the same and prevent multiple instantiations just like for invariant generics.
However, this is more restrictive than we need.  In fact, as long as we can identify some minimal instance
we can ensure type safety. 

To see why, consider the {\it head} function on the covariant list type ${\tt CoList}\ob{X}$.  Additionally,
we specialize it for some type {\tt A}.\\

$\begin{array}{l}
{\it coHead}\ob{X}({\tt CoList}\ob{X}) :X~(*){\it def1}\\
{\it coHead}\ob{Y <: {\tt A}}({\tt CoList}\ob{Y}) : Y~(*){\it def2}\\
\end{array}$\\

Note that we must make {\it def2} generic.  This is for the same reasons as the {\it polyOk} example above.
Consider the type {\tt B} unrelated to but not excluding {\tt A} and ${\tt C} <: \{ {\tt A}, {\tt B}\}$.  The type
${\tt AmbiguousCoList} <: \{ {\tt CoList}\ob{A}, {\tt CoList}\ob{B} \}$ causes the {\it coHead} overload to fail the 
return type rule.  Type parameter $X$ of {\it def1} can be instantiated to {\tt B} and since {\tt B} is not a subtype
of {\tt A}, there is no way to instantiate $Y$ of {\it def2} to be both applicable and type safe.  However, if we add
${\tt CoList}\ob{C}$ to make the type ${\tt OkCoList} <: \{ {\tt CoList}\ob{A}, {\tt CoList}\ob{B} {\tt CoList}\ob{C} \}$,
then the problem goes away since we can now choose to instantiate {\it def2} at {\tt C} and return ${\tt C} <: {\tt B}$
which is sound.

Thus, to multiple instantiation exclusion, we add that if the type parameter is covariant, then a type can extend multiple
instantiations of that type parameter as long as there exists a minimal instantiation that is a subtype of all other instantiations.
This is the ancestor meet rule that appears in the failed OOPSLA 2012 submission.

\subsubsection{Cross Instantiation}

There is one more problematic situation that we did not encounter with invariant type parameters.  Consider the
type ${\tt CoArrayList}\ob{X} <: {\tt CoList}\ob{X}$ which holds for all $X$.  Now, we specialize {\it coTail} for
the array list case:\\

$\begin{array}{l}
{\it coTail}\ob{X}({\tt CoList}\ob{X}) :{\tt CoList}\ob{X}~(*){\it def1}\\
{\it coTail}\ob{Y}({\tt CoArrayList}\ob{Y}) : {\tt CoArrayList}\ob{Y}~(*){\it def2}\\
\end{array}$\\

We consider {\it def2} to be more specific as usual since it handles a subset of the inputs of {\it def1}.
Now, consider the type ${\tt CrossInstance} <: \{ {\tt CoArrayList}\ob{{\tt Object}}, {\tt CoList}\ob{{\tt Number}} \}$.
This type provides a counter example to the return type rule for the {\it coTail} overload.  We can instantiate
{\it def1} to {\tt Number}, but in order to make {\it def2} applicable, we must instantiate it at {\tt Object} and
{\tt Object} is a not a subtype of {\tt Number}.

In light of this problem, we must add a second restriction to prevent these crossed instantiations.  

\begin{quote}
Given type ${\tt T}\ob{X}$ where $X$ is covariant and type ${\tt S}\ob{Y}$ were $Y$ is covariant and for all $Z$
${\tt S}\ob{Z} <: {\tt T}\ob{Z}$. Let {\tt A} and {\tt B} be distinct ground types where ${\tt A} <: {\tt B}$.  If
$I <: {\tt S}\ob{B}$ and $I <: {\tt T}\ob{A}$, then $I <: {\tt S}\ob{A}$.
\end{quote}

With these two restrictions, we can prove that special case overloads involving covariant type parameters 
will now pass the return type rule as well (TODO).

\subsubsection{Exception for selfless types}

This restriction is problematic for expressing certain types of relationships such as the numeric hierarchy
that is expressed using the so called self-type idiom (now selfless types or trolls). Some sets of numbers
and the operators over them give rise to special algebraic properties known as rings and the more specialized fields.  Fortress
aims to support them in the following way:\\

$\begin{array}{l}
{\bf trait}~{\tt Ring}\ob{X <: {\tt Number}}~{\bf comprises}~X~\dots~{\bf end}\\
{\bf trait}~{\tt Field}\ob{X <: {\tt Number}}~{\bf comprises}~X~{\bf extends}~{\tt Ring}\ob{X}~\dots~{\bf end}
\end{array}$\\

The self-type idiom is realized with the {\bf comprises} clause which contains the instantiation of the self type.
The {\bf comprises} clause limits the types that can extend the given type to those appearing in the clause.
In this idiomatic usage, the type ${\tt Ring}\ob{X}$ is identified as $X$.  Thus a ${\tt Field}\ob{\mathbb{Q}}$
is really just $\mathbb{Q}$ itself.

Unfortunately, the numerical hierarchy contains crossed instantiations of the kind that we determined
must be outlawed:\\

$\begin{array}{l}
{\bf trait}~\mathbb{Q}~{\bf extends}~{\tt Field}\ob{\mathbb{Q}}~\ldots~{\bf end}\\
{\bf trait}~\mathbb{Z}~{\bf extends}~\{ \mathbb{Q}, {\tt Ring}\ob{\mathbb{Z}}\}~\ldots~{\bf end}\\
\end{array}$\\

A $\mathbb{Z}$ is a ${\tt Field}\ob{\mathbb{Q}}$ and a ${\tt Ring}\ob{\mathbb{Z}}$ but not
a ${\tt Field}\ob{\mathbb{Z}}$ which breaks our rule given above.  As above, we can come
up with an example that is unsound if we allow this type hierarchy.\\

$\begin{array}{l}
{\it add}\ob{X}({\tt Ring}\ob{X}, {\tt Ring}\ob{X}) :{\tt Ring}\ob{X}~(*){\it def1}\\
{\it add}\ob{Y}({\tt Field}\ob{Y},{\tt Field}\ob{Y}) : {\tt Field}\ob{Y}~(*){\it def2}\\
\end{array}$\\

Take type $\mathbb{Z}$ which is provided as the inputs to {\it add}.  Both {\it def1} and {\it def2}
are applicable.  But if we instantiate {\it def1}
at $\mathbb{Z}$, then we have a return type of ${\tt Ring}\ob{\mathbb{Z}}$ for the less specific
definition.  The more specific {\it def2} is only applicable when instantiated at $\mathbb{Q}$, but the
resulting return type ${\tt Field}\ob{\mathbb{Q}}$ is not a subtype of ${\tt Ring}\ob{\mathbb{Z}}$,
thus witnessing the failure of the return type rule.

Recall that the return type rule handles two failure cases: first, the possibility that more specific
type information at runtime will cause a more specific function definition to be chosen.  Second
is that the more specific function may not be visible to the compiler (hidden behind an API).  Note
that the first failure case should not actually apply here.  When we statically know that we have
a ${\tt Ring}\ob{\mathbb{Z}}$, we actually know much more than this.  The self-type idiom means
that this type is equivalent to $\mathbb{Z}$.  But $\mathbb{Z} <: \mathbb{Q} <: {\tt Field}\ob{\mathbb{Q}}$
which implies that based on static information {\it def2} should apply.  However, this does not extend to
the second failure case when the more specific definition is hidden.

One way to ensure that the first situation cannot happen is to rewrite the overload so that the self-type
is a bound rather than the parameter type:\\

$\begin{array}{l}
{\it add}\ob{X <:{\tt Ring}\ob{X}}(X,X) : X~(*){\it def1}\\
{\it add}\ob{Y <: {\tt Field}\ob{Y}}(Y,Y) : Y~(*){\it def2}\\
\end{array}$\\

This forces us to recognize the type ${\tt Ring}\ob{\mathbb{Z}}$ as $\mathbb{Z}$ in order for {\it def1} to
apply which will automatically also mean that {\it def2} applies.  This approach suggests further that
the self-type idiom should be more than simply an idiom and instead a separate construct which cannot
be used as a first class type, but instead only in bounds.  Victor and John have started working on this
sort of theory with their {\it trolls}.  However, the visibility problem shows that this is not sufficient to fix the
unsoundness problems with the cross instantiation.  Therefore, more work needs to be done in order
to understand how to best support the numerical hierarchy in the Fortress type system.

92	- P-85 **The array design's three questions are open, with no default, and return after the switch-over with the array decisions A, B and D.** The array design is the compiled path's design for arrays. The three questions: whether the array factory chooses a store for each element type; whether the store also keeps the size as a field, beside the size in the type; and whether a factory for a size known only at run time returns the unsized `Array[\E,I\]`, whose type holds no size. These questions are apart from decisions A, B and D: decision A is how an `RR64` array made through the library's generic array traits gets the `double[]` store (P-84), B is where unboxed arithmetic happens, and D is the sizes in the model's own types (P-87). The whole preparation for the array work is to be done before the switch-over; only the work itself waits.
93	- P-87 **The model's text is the notation, and the vocabulary is repaired around it.** The model is microGPT's two programs; the vocabulary is the array operations that they are written in (`FlatArrays.fss` for C4, the flat program, and `FlatArrays2.fss` for the APL-style one). No operator in the model is replaced by a function call to pass an overload check, as a proposed repair once wrote `planeSum(mask, x)` for `mask + x`; the vocabulary changes instead. Decision D, still open and returning after the switch-over with the other array decisions (P-85), is such a diff: it gives C4's arrays sized types, in its vocabulary's signatures and in the model lines that these force (`explorations/reviews/decision-d-diff.md`; the patch itself is only in git, in the parent of `84aef6a4f`). Nothing of decision D is applied before microGPT compiles, after the switch-over.
94	- P-88 **The model's vocabulary leaves `+`, `-` and `MAX` between an array and a scalar to the library's scalar-extension block, and its diagonal keeps its own product.** The vocabulary, the array operations that microGPT is written in, declares none of these six operators, an array with a number on either side; the library's scalar-extension block, in `Library/FortressLibrary.fss`, serves them. `Diag`, the vocabulary's diagonal matrix, extends `Matrix` and overrides `mul`, the method that the library's matrix product calls, so `diag(v) m` scales the rows of `m` without forming the matrix. This is what the type system promises: a diagonal is a kind of matrix, with a faster product of its own. Row 299 records what the general product costs on a diagonal: 13 to 54 times as much as scaling the rows. Since the diagonal is read-only, a read-only matrix trait, `ReadableArray2`, which `Array2` would extend as `Array1` extends `ReadableArray1`, is also wanted (row 798): it is a library change, not a definition in the vocabulary.
95	- P-89 **`fill` takes a value, `tabulate` a function.** On the library's arrays, `fill(v)` fills an array with the value `v`, even when `v` is a function, and `tabulate(f)` fills it with `f` applied to each index. The function form, formerly an overload of `fill`, takes Scala's name `tabulate`. Why: in every peer language that has `fill`, `fill` takes the value.
96	- P-90 **`Maybe`'s empty case is the team's parametric `Nothing[\T\]`, in the one library and the specification.** The bare `Nothing` is future work: it needs a `where` clause that binds a type variable in an `extends` clause, which neither path implements, and it is not tried before then. Gating row 331 on static-argument inference instead is parked.
97	- P-91 **What an object with no `asString` prints: its bare Fortress type name, walk's spelling, on both paths.** An object with no `asString` of its own prints its Fortress type name as walk spells it, such as `Box`, or `Box[\ZZ32\]` for an instance of a generic object, with no marker and no hash code. A debug marker, such as the Java class name that the curator first leaned to, belongs in `asDebugString` if one is still wanted, not in the printed form; walk's `asDebugString` prints `a Box: Box`. Row 363: an `asDebugString` that prints as walk's does, where the compiled one prints `Box`. Row 321: printing an object that declares or inherits a zero-argument member named `toString`, which overflows the stack. Once the compiled path reads the one library, every object inherits such a member, the `getter toString` of that library's `trait Object`, so every object with no `asString` meets the overflow.
98	
99	### The specification's revision
100	
101	- P-95 **Every change to the specification is recorded with its reason.** When the revival changes the language, it updates `Specification/` with the change, so that the text and the implementation do not disagree. The original text and the reasoning are kept, so that route C stays open. Route C is the design that P-43 set aside: a nested number tower, under the forest rule of the team's 2012 patent applications (F-46 gives what a return to it would need). Every such change takes the revision form (P-96 gives its parts). The unrevised copy, `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, is never touched. Why: an open disagreement between the text and the implementation would confuse a reader.
102	- P-96 **A change of the specification is shown in layers, as the team showed its own changes in the 1.0 release of 2008 and in the working draft of 2009.** This form is the revision form. A callout that prints in every build marks each changed passage; a `\note` will not do, since a release build hides it. Appendix I's revival section has an entry for each change: its reason, its original text, what a return to route C would mean for it, or that it would be the same under route C (P-95 says what route C is), and the decision that it follows. The front matter has one paragraph on the revision, and a document in the repository holds the full reasoning. Citations call the unrevised copy, `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, the Working Draft of February 2011: the copy is that draft byte for byte, and only its `fortress.1.0.pdf` is the 1.0 release (F-163). The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/specification.md` gives each part in full, including what else an Appendix I entry holds.
103	- P-97 **The specification's examples that break the exclusion rule take the library's shapes, and each original stays, marked "Not allowed".** The Working Draft offered such examples as legal. Each now shows the shape that the library uses for the same thing, with the original beside it under the specification's own mark, "Not allowed". The specification states the rule, which it calls instantiation exclusion, once, in the two parts of Luchangco's Types chapter of 2012 (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`; P-25): `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex` says which instantiations exclude each other, and `basic/traits.tex` says that a declaration may not extend two that do. The covariance example, a trait that extends other instantiations of itself, is rewritten and marked in the same way. Its callout adds one sentence: the type group's later design, in the same Types chapter, declares variance with a `covariant` modifier, which neither walk nor the compiled path implements (row 404 records the gap). The calculi of Appendix A keep their rules as the team wrote them, under a callout that they predate the rule.
104	- P-98 **`TotalComparison` extends `StandardMinMax[\TotalComparison\]`, so that the library's `BIG MIN` and `BIG MAX` work over total comparisons.** It does so in the library's api and component, `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` and `.fss`. It keeps the five members that it restates by hand: `MIN`, `MAX`, `MINMAX`, `<=` and `>=`. Without the parent, walk finds no overload of `BIG MIN` or `BIG MAX` that takes total comparisons (row 461). Why: it is the library's own device, which its other ordered types use. The curator took it on the coordinator's recommendation. It stands and blocks no work.
105	
106	### The suites and the gate
107	
108	- P-102 **Test first, the test kept.** Every edit of source code in the original tree starts from a failing test. The worker adds the test to the test suite, sees it fail, makes the fix, and sees it pass. The test then stays in the suite for good. An edit of the specification or of documentation is not source code and needs no test. The gate's three test runs, `ant testFast`, `ant testSystem` and `ant testSpecData` (P-124), must pass when the work lands; they need not pass after every edit. The test and the fix may land in one commit. Why: the rule replaces one-off validation scripts, which no later build runs. The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/tests-writing.md` says how to write the test.
109	- P-103 **The suite's verdict is the check.** A test's result is pass or fail, as the team designed the suites. A value that matters is checked inside the test, with the checks that the harness already has: an `assert` call in an interpreter test, a `run_out_equals` key in a compiled test's `.test` file. What a test prints beyond its checks does not count. So no expected-output files are added. They are not proposed to the curator again, and neither is a comparison of what a test prints beyond its checks with an earlier run's output. Why: when the suite's designers let a test pass without a further check, what it prints need not be checked.
110	- P-124 **The specification's examples are a step of the gate, and every one must pass.** `ant testSpecData` runs the examples extracted from `Specification/` under walk (F-114 says which 130 it runs), and the gate fails if any of them fails. When an example fails, the implementation is fixed: the example is not respelled to get around a gap in walk, and no list of examples allowed to fail is kept.
111	- P-125 **The suites run Fortress in parallel, pinned at four threads in `build.xml`.** `build.xml` sets `FORTRESS_THREADS` to 4 for the two suites, `ant testFast` and `ant testSystem`, so that every run of them uses four threads, whatever the calling shell sets. A test that parallelism makes fail, on every run or only on some, is written wrong, for example a write that needs `atomic`, or it shows a defect. Either is fixed, never hidden by running at one thread. Why: Fortress is parallel by default, so a suite at one thread has a blind spot, and sparing the four-CPU machine is no reason for one.
112	- P-150 **No resident compiler is built.** A background JVM that serves Fortress commands, as Scala 2's `fsc` did, would save too little of the workers' time to be worth building (F-234), so the speed work goes to the checker itself (P-148). It is not tried again unless something significant changes.

Line \ref{generic} invokes {\sc match} to ensure that the lower bound of $P_j$ is structurally able to be a subtype of each declared upper bound $\xi$, and to propagate necessary bounds to other type parameters that have not yet been checked and inferred. 

If the match and propagation processes complete successfully, then $l_j$ is the type inferred for $P_j$, and the dispatch semipredicate returns the substitution $\substb{l}{P}$.

3944:\subsection{The type of \KWD{self} in a trait with a self-type parameter}
4062:\subsection{Passages not yet revised}
=== changes.tex 3944-4065 ===
\subsection{The type of \KWD{self} in a trait with a self-type parameter}
\seclabel{revival-self-type}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{idn-ref}; \secref{trait-decls}; \secref{methods}.
\item[Change] In \secref{idn-ref}, a sentence after the one on the self-type
idiom: in a declaration of a trait \VAR{T} with no \KWD{comprises} clause, or one that lists only ``\EXP{\ldots}'', and a
self-type parameter \VAR{X}, \KWD{self} has the type \EXP{T \cap X} in the bodies of
the trait's methods, and the \KWD{self} parameter keeps the type \VAR{T} in the
signature of each method declaration.
In \secref{trait-decls}, a paragraph after the one on \KWD{comprises} clauses
defines a self-type parameter: a static parameter of a trait with no
\KWD{comprises} clause, or one that lists only ``\EXP{\ldots}'', that is bounded by the trait at its own static
parameters, or by an instantiation of a trait with a self-type parameter that the
trait also lists in its \KWD{extends} clause, with that static parameter as the
static argument for the self-type parameter.
The paragraph requires every trait or object declaration and every object
expression that extends an instantiation of such a trait to be a subtype of
the static argument of that instantiation for the self-type parameter, a trait
standing as the type of \KWD{self} in its bodies, the intersection of its type with the types
its \KWD{comprises} clause lists or with its own self-type parameter, and gives an example marked ``Not allowed''.
In \secref{methods}, a box after the sentence that a functional method's
\KWD{self} parameter implicitly has the type of the enclosing trait or object
says that the sentence still holds of the declaration's signature.
Each of the three passages has a box.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; it follows the
revival's decision of 13~October 2026 on the bodies of the self-typed traits,
and its second form of a self-type parameter, through a trait that the trait
extends, follows a default taken under that decision on 14~October 2026.
\library\ declare their orders and their algebra as traits whose static
parameter is bounded by the trait itself, as in
\EXP{\KWD{trait}\;\TYP{Integral}\llbracket{}I \KWD{extends} \TYP{Integral}\llbracket{}I\rrbracket\rrbracket},
and give them default bodies that return \KWD{self} where that parameter is
declared, or pass it where the parameter is expected: the team's minimal
complete definitions, such as \OPR{MIN} on \TYP{StandardTotalOrder} and
\VAR{floor} on \TYP{Integral}.
The interpreter runs them; the compiled type checker refused 29 of them,
since it typed \KWD{self} as the trait.
A bound constrains the static argument, not \KWD{self}: an object may extend
\EXP{\TYP{Integral}\llbracket\mathbb{Z}32\rrbracket} without being a
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and a body that treats \KWD{self} as the parameter is sound
only if every declaration that extends the trait is a subtype of its static
argument for that parameter.
Scala states that rule for its declared self types (``The self type of a class
or object must conform to the self types of all classes which are inherited by
the template'', \emph{Scala Language Specification 2.13}, section 5.1); the revival reads the self type from the bound, which \library\
already write, as the team's compiled type checker reads it from a
\KWD{comprises} clause (\secref{idn-ref}), a reading that the team's gated test
\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXX10k.test} pins.
Naden's account of the Return Type Rule (2012) asked that the self-type idiom
become ``a separate construct which cannot be used as a first class type, but
instead only in bounds''
(\nolinkurl{Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex}, lines 626--630).
The signatures keep the type of the trait because the type group's account of
overloading of 2019 (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu, POPL 2019) assumes, for the
completeness of its matching of types, that no declared type holds a type
parameter inside an intersection (pp.~11:21--22), and its Return Type Rule
compares declared domains (p.~11:13): with the intersection in the signatures,
the domains of the two declarations of \OPR{CMP} on \TYP{StandardPartialOrder}
and \TYP{StandardTotalOrder} became equivalent, and the compiled type checker
reported 18 errors of the Return Type Rule that the declarations do not make.
The second form of a self-type parameter keeps valid as written the mixins of
\library\ that the team wrote in 2009, \TYP{ContainmentBySubset} and
\TYP{ContainmentByComparison}, whose static parameter is bounded by the trait
\TYP{Containment}, which they extend at it.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/self-typed-bodies-judgement.md} and
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-self-type/decision-record.md} in the
revival's repository.
\item[Effect] The compiled type checker types \KWD{self} as \EXP{T \cap X} in
the bodies of the dotted and functional methods of a trait with a self
parameter \VAR{X}, keeps \VAR{T} in the signatures that overloading, the Return
Type Rule and the choice of a declaration at a call read, and refuses a trait
or object declaration or an object expression that the new paragraph of
\secref{trait-decls} does not allow, with the message
``\VAR{D} extends \EXP{C\llbracket{}A\rrbracket}, whose self parameter is \VAR{A},
but \VAR{D} is not a subtype of \VAR{A}.''.
The interpreter has no static types: it runs the bodies as before, and loads a
declaration that the paragraph refuses.
The code generator compiles a default body that returns \KWD{self} as the self
parameter with no conversion to the type of the instance, so a program that
runs such a body, which the compiled type checker now accepts, with the parameter at an object type
fails the JVM's verification when the body's class is loaded (row~695 of the revival's gap
ledger).
\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/var-ref.tex},
lines 53--54 and 64--69, which stand unchanged and are now followed by the new
sentence:
\begin{quote}
The type of \KWD{self} is the type of the trait or object being declared by
the innermost enclosing trait or object declaration or object expression.
\end{quote}
and
\begin{quote}
If the innermost enclosing such construct is a trait declaration (for a trait
called, say, `\EXP{T}'), and that trait declaration has a \KWD{comprises}
clause, and `\EXP{U_1}', `\EXP{U_2}', ..., `\EXP{U_n}' are the traits mentioned
in the \KWD{comprises} clause, then the type of \KWD{self} is instead
``\EXP{T \cap (U_{\mathrm{1}} \cup U_{\mathrm{2}} \cup \ldots \cup U_{\mathrm{n}})}''.
\end{quote}
The paragraph of \secref{trait-decls} is new.
\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/traits.tex}, line 486, the end of the
sentence of \secref{methods} that the new box follows, stands unchanged:
\begin{quote}
and implicitly has the type of the enclosing trait or object.
\end{quote}
\item[Route C] Under route~C a self-typed trait is read by a \KWD{comprises}
clause that lists its static parameter, as the compiled path's own library
declares its orders (\nolinkurl{Library/CompilerAlgebra.fsi}, lines 16 and 24,
in the revival's repository); under such a clause the self-type idiom of
\secref{idn-ref} types \KWD{self}, and this rule is not reached.
A return to that form would need the clause on the self-typed traits of
\library, which would also close each of them to its static parameter; a way
for the interpreter past its stack overflow on a clause that lists a static
parameter (row~407 of the revival's gap ledger); and leave in
\secref{trait-decls} for a static parameter as a listed type, which the type
group's calculus of 2012 does not admit.
\end{description}

\subsection{Passages not yet revised}
\seclabel{revival-notrevised}

A trait has a \emph{trait type} of the same name.}

A trait type is a subtype of every type
that appears in the \KWD{extends} clause of its definition.
In addition, every trait type is a subtype of \TYP{Any}.

A trait declaration may also include an \KWD{excludes} clause,
in which case the defined trait type
excludes every type that appears in that clause.
Every trait type also excludes every arrow type and every tuple type,
and the special types \TYP{()} and \TYP{BottomType}.

\subsection{Object Trait Types}
\seclabel{object-traits}

An object trait type is a trait type defined by an object declaration.
Object declarations do not include \KWD{excludes} clauses,
but an object trait type cannot be extended.
Thus, an object trait type excludes any type that is not its supertype.

\section{Object Expression Types}
\seclabel{object-exp-types}

An object expression type is defined by an object expression
(described in \secref{object-expr})
and the program location of the object expression.
Every evaluation of a given object expression has the same
object expression type.  Two object expressions at different program locations
have different object expression types.

Like trait types,
an object expression type is a subtype of all trait types
that appear in the \KWD{extends} clause of its definition,
as well as the type \TYP{Any}.

Like object trait types,
an object expression type excludes any type that is not its supertype.


\section{Tuple Types}
\seclabel{tuple-types}

\begin{Grammar}
\emph{TupleType} &::=&
\texttt{(} \emph{Type}\EXP{,} \emph{TypeList} \texttt{)}\\

\emph{TypeList} &::=& \emph{Type}(\EXP{,} \emph{Type})$^*$

of two or more types.

Every tuple type is a subtype of \TYP{Any}.
No other type encompasses all tuple types.
Tuple types cannot be extended by trait types.
Tuple types are covariant:
a tuple type $X$ is a subtype of tuple type $Y$
if and only if they have the same number of element types
and each element type of $X$ is a subtype of the
corresponding element type of $Y$.

A tuple type excludes any non-tuple type
other than \TYP{Any}.
A tuple type excludes every tuple type that does not have the same
number of element types.
Also, tuple types that have the same number of element types exclude each other
if any pair of corresponding element types exclude each other.

Intersection of nonexclusive tuple types are defined elementwise; the
